text: Advertisement Last year, Mickael Mauger got his hands on a tiny electrical switch unlike any he had ever seen. Dr. Mauger is in the business of building equipment that pumps electricity into the world’s computer data centers . This requires specialized switches that can detect a dangerous power surge and shut down the flow of electricity. But these circuit breakers are always flawed. Dr. Mauger had to choose between an old-fashioned mechanical switch the size of a baseball, which is painfully slow, and a superfast sliver of a switch built from silicon, which wastes enormous amounts of electricity. Then he discovered a switch that was fast, efficient and small enough to sit on the end of his index finger. When he spoke to the company that made it, he asked, “How is this even possible?” This unusual device came from a start-up called Atomic Machines, which is taking a new approach to industrial design and manufacturing. Drawing on the power of artificial intelligence, the company is building what it calls a “matter compiler” — an automated manufacturing system that turns computer code into a physical device, much like a software compiler that transforms code into a working software application. The components of Atomic Machines’s electrical switch are so small that they can be viewed only through a microscope. Credit... Christie Hemm Klok for The New York Times Image The company’s switch can handle up to 150 amps of continuous current, enough to charge three Teslas at the same time. Credit...
